{{Short description|American chemist and civil liberties activist}}
'''Julian Phillip Heicklen''' (March 9, 1932 – March 11, 2022) was an American chemist and civil liberties activist.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/20/obituaries/julian-heicklen-dead.html|title=Julian Heicklen, Cantankerous Civil Liberties Advocate, Dies at 90|first=Clay|last=Risen|date=March 20, 2022|via=NYTimes.com}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Heicklen was born on March 9, 1932, in [[Rochester, New York]].<ref name="auto"> {{Cite news |last=Risen |first=Clay |date=2022-03-20 |title=Julian Heicklen, Cantankerous Civil Liberties Advocate, Dies at 90 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/20/obituaries/julian-heicklen-dead.html |access-date=2024-07-05 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} </ref> 

Heicklen received a BA in chemical engineering from [[Cornell University]] in 1954. He received a PhD in chemistry from the [[University of Rochester]] in 1958.<ref name="auto"/>

==Career==
After receiving his PhD, Heicklen moved to Los Angeles to work for a defense contractor.<ref name="auto"/>

Heicklen became a professor at [[Pennsylvania State University]] in 1967. He was well liked by the students for his unorthodox style of instruction. To increase interest in his classes, he would hand [[Out Campaign|out campaign]] buttons and appear in class wearing a cape. To demonstrate chemical reactions, he invited school gymnasts. He retired in 1992.<ref name="auto"/>

==Activism==
While working in Los Angeles, Heicklen became active in the local chapter of the [[Congress of Racial Equality]]. He was involved in activism throughout his teaching career but became more active after his retirement.<ref name="auto"/> After he retired in the early 1990s, he openly smoked marijuana in public in [[State College, Pennsylvania]], as a protest against marijuana laws and to intentionally be arrested, which happened about five times. He did not smoke marijuana recreationally and did so only as a protest.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/02/26/nyregion/26jury.html|title=Jury Nullification Advocate Is Indicted|first=Benjamin|last=Weiser|date=February 25, 2011|via=NYTimes.com}}</ref>

Heicklen was arrested multiple times by U.S. [[Department of Homeland Security]] federal police officers while distributing [[Fully Informed Jury Association]] (FIJA) literature at the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]].

On May 25, 2010, he was arrested after refusing to stop handing out pamphlets about jury nullification at a [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York|U.S. District Courthouse in New York City]], and was indicted for [[jury tampering]]. Because of previous failures to appear in court, he was remanded to [[Rikers Island]] until his June 8 arraignment.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://jailedactivist.info/activists/julian-heicklen/ |title=Jailed Activist Info » Julian Heicklen |accessdate=2010-06-08 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100531001755/http://jailedactivist.info/activists/julian-heicklen/ |archivedate=2010-05-31 }}</ref>  His arrest gained national attention over the following year due to the [[First Amendment]] implications of arresting a citizen for handing out educational pamphlets.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/11/28/nyregion/brief-details-jury-nullification-case-against-julian-heicklen.html?scp=1&sq=Julian%20Heicklen&st=cse | work=The New York Times | first=Benjamin | last=Weiser | title=Brief Details Jury Nullification Case Against Julian Heicklen | date=November 27, 2011}}</ref>

Heicklen was arrested or fined multiple times related to distributing pamphlets on nullificiation. Heicklen wrote that during one arrest he chose to fall to the ground limp and silent; an ambulance was called and he signed his hospital release form as "[[John Galt]]."<ref>{{citation|publisher=American Juror|title=FIJA Demonstrations in New York|date=Autumn 2009|author=Heicklen, Julian|url=http://fija.org/docs/NL_2009_v21_n3-4.pdf|access-date=2013-06-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161020040135/http://fija.org/docs/NL_2009_v21_n3-4.pdf|archive-date=2016-10-20|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Another activist was arrested for filming on federal property without permission while recording Heicklen's November 9, 2009 arrest.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.empirestatenews.net/News/20100426-3.html |title=New York State News on the Net! |accessdate=2010-05-06 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723115811/http://www.empirestatenews.net/News/20100426-3.html |archivedate=2011-07-23 }}</ref> Fellow nullification activists held a protest in his defense.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wfmz.com/news/23797465/detail.html |title=Group Protests Arrest of Activist - News Story - WFMZ Allentown |accessdate=2010-06-08 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100607043733/http://www.wfmz.com/news/23797465/detail.html |archivedate=2010-06-07 }}</ref>

On April 19, 2012, District Court Judge [[Kimba Wood]] granted Heicklen's Motion to Dismiss the Indictment as legally deficient.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.constitution.org/jury/pj/10-cr-01154-KMW_order.pdf|title=UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT - SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF NEW YORK: UNITED STATES OF AMERICA - v. - JULIAN HEICKLEN}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/04/20/nyregion/indictment-against-julian-heicklen-jury-nullification-advocate-is-dismissed.html|title=Jury Statute Not Violated by Protester, Judge Rules|first=Benjamin|last=Weiser|date=April 20, 2012|via=NYTimes.com}}</ref>

<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/11/28/nyregion/brief-details-jury-nullification-case-against-julian-heicklen.html|title=Prosecution Explains Jury Tampering Charge|first=Benjamin|last=Weiser|date=November 28, 2011|via=NYTimes.com}}</ref>
